body_markdown:
AI agents executing complex workflows may need to combine operational and analytical data, persistent memory, semantic retrieval, and access to tools within a single reasoning loop. Together, these services make up the agent data stack. When teams build that stack from separate services, they have to integrate each service and keep copied data in sync, or else their agents will act on stale information. At its October event in Fort Lauderdale, Couchbase outlined a multimodel, multicapability convergence strategy designed to bring more of this stack onto its operational data platform.


New capabilities include managed agent memory, tool connectivity, model access, and a translytical bridge between analytical insights and operational action. As agentic AI matures, operational data platforms are becoming critical infrastructure for agent context, reasoning, and execution.


### **Couchbase Moves Agent Memory Into A Managed Service**


Couchbase is making Agent Memory available as a fully managed service starting with AWS, in addition to its existing self-managed deployment. Through one API, developers can now manage conversation history, user profiles, and semantically searchable facts, including context limited to the current session and information retained across sessions. The service includes time-based retrieval, time-to-live and deletion controls, access tracing, user-level isolation, and support for multiple agent frameworks. As agents retain memory across sessions, that memory becomes a new category of enterprise data requiring governance. Data teams must establish who can access it, how its provenance is tracked, how long it is retained, and how it can be corrected or deleted.


### **Couchbase Standardizes Agent Access To Data And Tools Through Managed MCP**


Couchbase’s managed Model Context Protocol (MCP) server on AWS gives compatible agents and applications a standard way to reach live operational data and Couchbase tools. The tools cover data work, such as schema discovery, document operations, and SQL queries, along with cluster administration (including index management, cluster health, and query performance analysis). All tools run read-only by default. Administrators can disable individual tools or require confirmation before sensitive actions, and the managed service supports role-based API keys and IP allow lists. Teams that connect many agents to one MCP server will need a separate API key for each agent — limited to the tools and data it requires — with read-write access granted only where a task demands it.


### **Couchbase Adds Vector Search And Write-Back To Operational Insights**


Couchbase has added vector search to Operational Insights, its analytical service for processing historical JSON data. In a single SQL call, teams can combine vector similarity with structured analysis: for example, by clustering customer reviews by meaning and relating those clusters to current order or manufacturing data — all with no ETL. Teams can then write the results back into the operational data that applications and agents use. This translytical pattern connects analysis with operational action, allowing results to be written back within the same platform. When an analytical result changes operational state directly, teams also need to trace each change to the analysis behind it, set oversight in proportion to risk, and keep a way to roll back or remediate a bad change.


### **Couchbase Targets Agent Economics Through Native Amazon Bedrock Integration**


Couchbase’s native Amazon Bedrock integration now gives customers pay-per-token access to language and embedding models, with semantic caching and no GPU infrastructure to manage. Customers can also use embedding models from their own Bedrock accounts over PrivateLink. Couchbase estimates 40–60% fewer model calls from semantic caching, 33–45% lower token use from Agent Memory, and prompts 70% smaller from concise vector query responses. These estimates matter only if buyers measure the end-to-end cost of each business task that an agent completes successfully at the quality, freshness, latency, and reliability that the task requires.


## What Enterprise Leaders Must Do


With these announcements, Couchbase moves agent memory, governed data, tool access, and write-back closer to the operational data that agents act on. Our upcoming research on the context layer groups the capabilities that enterprises need into modeling business context, serving it to applications and agents, and maintaining it as the business changes. Enterprises need operational data in each of these areas, because operational platforms hold business state and agents write their actions back to them. Start with these actions:


- **Model operational state and decision history alongside business meaning.** Represent the current state of key processes, data assets, and system dependencies, with source and update information so agents can assess whether the information is current enough for the task. Record decisions, as well, including the inputs, rules applied, exceptions, any required approval, and outcome, so people and agents can search past cases for relevant evidence. Review what agents already keep in memory to find decision-relevant information that should be validated and retained as a governed record.
- **Serve context through governed, open interfaces.** Give applications and agents access to business meaning, policies, operational state, and decision history through APIs and MCP interfaces. Authorize access and filter responses based on the identity of the requesting agent and, where applicable, the delegated permissions of the user it acts for. Apply consistent policies across every context source so that each application and agent framework receives context governed by the same access requirements.
- **Capture write-backs with their provenance.** When people, applications, or agents change operational data, record the action and associated decision as they occur and link outcomes as they become known. Link each record to the context, sources, and versions of the business definitions, policies, and rules used so that reviewers can explain the change and teams can refine the rules that agents follow.
- **Assign owners to keep context synchronized and current.** Ingest changes from systems of record and define source authority and conflict resolution rules for cases where sources disagree. Make named owners responsible for reviewing, versioning, retaining, and deleting context, including agent memory, on every platform that holds it. Monitor freshness, conflicts, drift, and usage so that teams can correct context or restrict agent action when information is stale or conflicts remain unresolved.
